chapters.title: Chapter 3: Chart Patterns on Currency Pairs

lessons.title: Why Forex Rarely Gaps (and What Happens When It Does): Weekend Gaps and News Spikes

children.text: A surprise US inflation number drops on a Wednesday evening. Rohit checks his EUR/USD chart the next morning expecting a dramatic gap, the way Nifty gaps up or down after big overnight news. There is no gap. The pair simply moved sharply, tick by tick, the moment the number was released. Two days later, on Monday, his USD/INR futures chart on NSE opens with a clean 40-paise gap from Friday's close, even though nothing unusual happened over the weekend. Rohit has run into the one genuinely reliable rule about gaps in forex: they depend entirely on whether trading actually stopped.

body.text: A gap needs a real stoppage in trading behind it. Spot forex trades continuously through the week, so it absorbs news tick by tick and rarely gaps on a weekday. It does stop once a week, over the weekend, and NSE's currency segment stops every single evening, which is why gaps on currency futures are a daily, expected feature rather than a rare event.

children.text: Why Weekday Gaps Are Rare on Spot Forex

A stock gaps because the exchange is shut overnight while news keeps happening, so the next open has to jump to catch up on everything that occurred while nobody could trade. Global spot EUR/USD has no such blackout during the week. From Monday's Sydney open to Friday's New York close, someone, somewhere, is always quoting a price, so a surprise inflation print or a shock statement gets priced in within seconds, as a sharp move on the chart, not as a jump between two candles.

cells: Very rare, since trading never stops during the week
The one structural gap every week, Friday's New York close to Monday's Sydney open
Common, a small gap most mornings between Friday's 5:00 pm close and the next 9:00 am open
The largest gap of the week, since it also carries the entire weekend's global move

body.title: Illustrative EUR/USD: Friday Close to Monday Open

children.text: This is an illustrative pattern, not a live quote. Friday's last real price is 1.0850. By the time Sydney opens Monday, the pair opens at 1.0790, a clean gap with no candles in between, because nobody was quoting EUR/USD anywhere in the world during that stretch. A weekend geopolitical development or a surprise central bank leak is exactly the kind of news that shows up this way, priced in all at once the moment trading resumes.

body.title: Sizing the weekend gap
body.prompt: Using the illustrative example above, EUR/USD closes Friday at 1.0850 and opens Monday at 1.0790. How large is the weekend gap, in pips? (1 pip equals 0.0001)
body.explanation: 1.0850 minus 1.0790 equals 0.0060, or 60 pips. A gap of this size over a weekend, with no scheduled data behind it, would usually be attributed to a geopolitical or unscheduled news development.

children.text: NSE's Monday Gap Is a Gap of a Gap

Here is the part traders on NSE currency futures regularly get wrong. USD/INR futures close Friday at 5:00 pm IST. Global spot markets then trade through the entire weekend gap and continue trading through Sydney and Tokyo's Monday sessions, from 2:30 am IST onward, a full six and a half hours before NSE even reopens at 9:00 am. Whatever the dollar has already done during those six and a half hours is baked into the rate well before the first NSE candle prints. Comparing Monday's NSE open only against Friday's NSE close, without checking what global spot did overnight and in the early Monday hours, will leave you guessing at a gap size that has nothing to do with what actually happened.

body.text: Before assuming a certain Monday gap on USD/INR futures, check a global dollar chart, such as the dollar index or EUR/USD, for what it did between Friday's New York close and Monday's early Asian hours. NSE's 9:00 am open reflects all of that accumulated move at once, not just the weekend headline you may have seen.

body.title: The gap that was bigger than expected
body.scenario: USD/INR futures close Friday at ₹95.20. Over the weekend, Priya reads that the US dollar strengthened broadly on a geopolitical development. She expects USD/INR to open perhaps 15 to 20 paise higher on Monday. Instead, NSE opens at ₹95.65, a 45-paise gap.
body.prompt: What did Priya most likely fail to account for, and what should she check before making this kind of estimate in future?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Priya likely estimated the gap only from the weekend headline, without checking how much the dollar had already moved in global spot trading between Friday's New York close and Monday's early Asian sessions.
2. Global markets, including Sydney and Tokyo, had already been trading USD strength for six and a half hours before NSE opened at 9:00 am, and that entire move gets absorbed into the opening print at once.
3. Before estimating an NSE gap, she should check a global dollar chart, such as the dollar index or EUR/USD, for its move from Friday's New York close through Monday's early Asian hours, not just react to a weekend news headline.
4. She should treat the NSE opening print as reflecting the full accumulated global move, not just the weekend event itself.

children.text: A true gap needs a stoppage in trading. But during an extreme, unscheduled shock, some brokers briefly widen spreads dramatically or pull quotes for a few seconds as liquidity providers step back, which can look like a small gap on your own chart even though the wider market never technically closed. The 2015 Swiss franc shock, covered in more depth in a dedicated case study elsewhere in this curriculum, is the best-known example of this kind of flash event, where quoted prices moved so violently and with such thin liquidity that many brokers effectively could not fill orders at any predictable price for a short period.

body.text: During an extreme, unscheduled news shock, do not assume your stop-loss will fill anywhere near the price you set it at. Widened spreads and thin liquidity during a flash event can cause severe slippage, filling your order far worse than expected, which is a real risk even though it does not show up on a chart as a textbook overnight gap.

children.text: A small weekend gap, driven by routine order imbalances rather than genuine news, often gets filled within the following day or two, as price drifts back to close the empty space on the chart. A large gap driven by a real fundamental shock, a surprise rate move or a geopolitical event that actually changes the outlook, is a different matter. It can represent a genuine repricing that never fully reverses, and treating every gap as something that must close is a good way to fight a real trend.

body.title: Which gap is more likely to fill quickly?
body.question: Which of these two weekend gaps is statistically more likely to be filled within the following few sessions?
options: A 10-pip gap on EUR/USD with no identifiable news behind it
A 300-pip gap on EUR/USD following a surprise central bank policy shift
Both are equally likely to fill
Neither type of gap ever fills
body.explanation: Small, noise-driven gaps with no real news behind them often fill quickly, since nothing fundamental actually changed. A large gap driven by a genuine policy shock can represent a real repricing and is far less reliable to trade purely on the assumption that gaps always close.

cards.definition: The difference between Friday's New York close and Monday's Sydney open on global spot forex, the one structural weekly gap on a continuously traded pair.

The situation on NSE currency futures where the Monday opening print reflects not just the weekend's global move but also several hours of Monday morning trading in Sydney and Tokyo that happened before NSE reopened.
A brief period of extreme volatility and thin liquidity, sometimes causing spreads to widen dramatically and orders to fill far from expected prices, without a true session close behind it.
When price retraces back to close an open gap on the chart. More likely for small, noise-driven gaps than for gaps caused by a genuine fundamental shock.

points: A gap requires a real stoppage in trading. Spot forex trades continuously through the week, so it rarely gaps on weekdays, but it always gaps once a week, over the weekend.
NSE currency futures gap daily, since the exchange genuinely closes each evening, and their Monday gap is the largest of the week because it also carries the weekend's global move.
Before estimating an NSE Monday gap, check a global dollar chart for what happened between Friday's New York close and Monday's early Asian hours, not just a weekend headline.
Extreme, unscheduled news shocks can cause flash events, widened spreads and severe slippage, even without a technical gap between candles.
Small, noise-driven gaps often fill quickly. Large gaps driven by genuine fundamental shocks can represent a real repricing and should not be traded purely on the assumption that gaps always close.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not trading advice. All chart examples are illustrative and not live or historical quotes. Gap behaviour is probabilistic, not guaranteed, and slippage risk during volatile events is real. Always use proper risk management and position sizing.
